prompt: In the derivation of the kinetic theory equation pV = (1/3) N m <c^2>, what physical justification leads to the factor of 1/3?
options: Molecular motion is isotropic in three dimensions, so the mean-square velocity component along any one axis is <c_x^2> = (1/3) <c^2>.
Each molecule collides with only one pair of opposite faces in a six-faced cubic container.
Collisions with the walls are elastic, so one-third of the momentum is transferred to each perpendicular wall.
The volume of the molecules occupies one-third of the total volume of the container.

answer.explanation: Because molecular motion is completely random (isotropic), <c^2> = <c_x^2> + <c_y^2> + <c_z^2> and <c_x^2> = <c_y^2> = <c_z^2>. Therefore, <c^2> = 3 <c_x^2>, giving <c_x^2> = (1/3) <c^2>.

distractor_explanations: Option 1 is correct: random 3D motion means velocity squared is equally distributed among the three Cartesian axes, <c_x^2> = (1/3) <c^2>.
Option 2 is incorrect: molecules move in three dimensions and collide with all faces over time.
Option 3 is incorrect: momentum change is 2mu perpendicular to the face; momentum is not split into thirds.
Option 4 is incorrect: molecular volume is assumed to be negligible, not one-third of the container.
hints: Think about resolving a 3D velocity vector into Cartesian components: c^2 = c_x^2 + c_y^2 + c_z^2.
What does the assumption of random motion tell you about the averages of these components?
solution: In three dimensions, Pythagoras' theorem gives c^2 = c_x^2 + c_y^2 + c_z^2. On average, because motion is completely random with no preferred direction, <c_x^2> = <c_y^2> = <c_z^2>. Thus, <c^2> = 3 <c_x^2>, which means <c_x^2> = (1/3) <c^2>. This introduces the factor of 1/3 when relating 1D wall collisions to total 3D mean-square speed. Option A is correct.
teacher_walkthrough: Apply symmetry: randomness ensures no axis is favoured, so all three component averages are equal.
Conclude that <c_x^2> = (1/3) <c^2> is the origin of the 1/3 factor.
